title: How good does a cloth simulator have to be before the laundry-robot hanger it designs is the right one?
lede: research programme: how much cloth-simulator fidelity and fabric data a laundry-robot hanger design loop needs before its choice holds on a validated solver; milestone 1, on four fabrics with published KES-FB bending rigidity and weight, finds the 2D chain and 3D sheet agree on every decision (wood-shaped hanger, arm 1 cm wider than the half shoulder) but agree to 0.004 cm because on a deep arm they are one model, and on a 3 cm arm the solver error (0.05 to 0.11 cm) is as large as the margin that picks the width (0.08 to 0.13 cm); milestone 1b solves the 3 cm arm to convergence and its best width moves to +1.5 cm on all four fabrics, against +1.0 cm in the 2D chain, a disagreement the 3000-iteration cap hid by flattering narrow arms; milestone 2a builds a simulated Cusick drape test on the 3D sheet: it orders the fabrics by bending length, but unmeasured stretch stiffness moves the drape coefficient 0.15 to 0.23 and, stiffened, every fabric drapes alike at about 0.77 (the spring grid locks), so drape cannot calibrate bending rigidity on this tier; milestone 1c reruns the 3 cm arm across stretch stiffness and mesh: the mesh leaves the width choice alone, but EA moves it from +2.0 to +2.5 cm at 40 N/m to +0.5 to +1.0 cm at 800 N/m while the 2D chain stays near +1.0 cm, so the tier disagreement changes sign with an unmeasured fabric property; milestone 2b refines the drape test's grid to 2.5 mm: the stiff suiting converges but the soft jersey does not above 150 N/m, and swapping springs shows most of the leftover stretch dependence is the shear spring the model ties to EA, a stiffness the same KES table measures (G = 26 to 89 N/m); milestone 1d sets the shear spring from measured G: stretch still moves the shallow-arm width by 1.0 cm across 40 to 800 N/m, but at 800 N/m and up, including the stiffness the KES tensile data imply, all four fabrics pick +1.0 cm, matching the 2D chain, so the tier disagreement is a soft-cloth effect and only the low-load tensile toe of the cotton jersey and shirting is left to measure; milestone 5 proves that a cheap tier's regret is bounded by how much its error varies across designs, not by its size, and finds that bound certifies no 2D-chain width (its error spreads 0.6 to 1.3 cm across widths against 0.05 to 0.25 cm margins, though the realised regret averages 0.03 cm), only a nearby stiffness guess, so the cheap tier can screen widths but not judge them; milestone 5b keeps the cheap tier's penalty term, a bound 2.8 times tighter on the 2D chain, and as a screen-and-verify loop (three reference runs around the cheap choice, then whatever the bound cannot rule out) finds the reference-tier best width in 48 of 50 tier pairs with 3.9 of 7 reference runs; milestone 3a builds ARCSim's triangle element with a Newton solver: it matches the exact cantilever elastica (within 0.9% of the overhang, extrapolated) but fails the Cusick acceptance test, locking on the soft jersey above EA 150 N/m and drifting 0.016 per refinement on the suiting; milestone 3b continues each stiff case from the soft equilibrium, all 40 converge, and at the jersey's sourced stiffness (254 and 369 N/m) the drape coefficient is flat in mesh (within 0.011) and stretch (0.003), so the jersey passes; the suiting misses by 0.004 to 0.006 through a fold-count change, and fold branches of one case differ by up to 0.32
summary: An open research programme on designing a laundry robot's hangers by cloth simulation: how much simulator fidelity and how much measured fabric data the design loop needs before the hanger it picks is still the best one on a validated, calibrated solver, and whether cheap models can certify that. The proposal reviews 19 works (cloth solvers, cloth parameter fitting, the cloth sim-to-real gap, multi-fidelity and robust design), states four falsifiable hypotheses and targets IEEE RA-L. Milestone 1 scores three stock hangers and five arm widths on four fabrics whose bending rigidity (0.0066 to 0.125 gf·cm²/cm) and weight are published KES-FB measurements, in three model tiers (2D chain, 3D sheet on a slab arm, 3D sheet on a 3 cm half-depth arm scored on the whole sheet). Every tier picks the wood-shaped hanger (0.38 to 0.47 cm RMS from the worn shape on the slab, against 3.1 to 3.4 cm for wire and plastic) and an arm 1 cm wider than the half shoulder on every fabric; the only ranking disagreement is a tie for second place. But on a deep arm the 2D and 3D errors differ by at most 0.004 cm, so their agreement is no test of fidelity, and on the 3 cm arm doubling the solver iterations moves the error by 0.05 to 0.11 cm, the same size as the 0.08 to 0.13 cm margin that decides the width. Milestone 1b solves those 3 cm-arm cases to convergence (12,000 to 24,000 iterations, error change under 0.002 cm per 3000). The best width moves to +1.5 cm on all four fabrics (on the 1 cm grid, +2 on fabric D), while the 2D chain stays sharply at +1.0 cm. The 3000-iteration bias depends on the width (+0.22 cm at −1 cm, −0.07 cm at +3 cm), so stopping early favoured narrow arms and made the tiers look as if they agreed. Simulation only: stretch stiffness (150 N/m) is assumed, garments are one size-M strip, there is no friction and no validated solver yet. Milestone 2a builds a simulated Cusick drape test (30 cm specimen on an 18 cm disc) on the same sheet, made isotropic in bending, and solves 140 cases to a drape-coefficient stopping rule. The drape coefficient orders the four fabrics by bending length (0.19, 0.21, 0.32, 0.45) with seed noise under 0.01, but the unmeasured stretch stiffness moves it by 0.15 to 0.23 (EA 40 against 800 N/m), shear by 0.08 to 0.11 and the mesh by up to 0.05; post hoc, stiffening the springs to 12,800 N/m lifts every fabric to about 0.77, so two fabrics with 19-fold different bending rigidity drape alike. That is membrane locking of the square spring grid: on this tier a measured drape coefficient cannot pin bending rigidity, so drape calibration moves to the validated top tier, whose first acceptance test is this one. No measured drape table could be reached this session. Milestone 1c reruns the converged 3 cm arm on fabrics A and D at EA 40, 150 and 800 N/m and two mesh changes (70 cases, all converged, predictions committed first): the mesh keeps the +1.5 cm choice, but the 3D sheet's best width goes from +2.0 to +2.5 cm at EA 40 to +0.5 to +1.0 cm at EA 800, while the 2D chain stays at +1.0 cm (+1.5 for fabric D at EA 40). The 3D-against-2D disagreement therefore runs from +1.0 to −0.5 cm with a stretch stiffness the KES-FB2 table does not give: on a shallow arm, bending rigidity and weight do not pick the hanger on this tier, and measured tensile data is a precondition for calibration. Milestone 2b refines the drape test's spring grid from 7.5 to 2.5 mm (26 cases, predictions committed first). The stiff suiting converges to about 0.01, but the soft jersey does not at EA 800 N/m and up (0.70 to 0.37 at EA 3200, still falling), and the overhang barely compresses at any EA (under 0.15%). A post hoc swap shows the sheet's shear spring, tied to EA at 0.1, carries most of the leftover dependence: on the suiting at 2.5 mm, shear alone (80 to 320 N/m) raises DC by 0.046 and stretch alone (800 to 3200 N/m) by 0.027; on the jersey, 0.139 against 0.013. Shear rigidity is measured in the same KES table as B and W (G = 0.47 to 1.58 gf/cm/deg, 26 to 89 N/m per radian), so it can now be set from data; the shallow-arm width shift of milestone 1c uses the same coupling and is the next thing to recheck. Milestone 1d reruns that shallow-arm choice with the shear spring set from each fabric's measured G and stretch stiffness swept on its own (126 converged cases, 4 fabrics). Shear was a third of milestone 1c's effect: EA 40 to 800 N/m still moves the best width by 1.0 cm (+2.0 to +1.0) on both the jersey and the suiting. But from 800 N/m up, including a secant stiffness derived from the same table's tensile LT and WT (2,360 to 15,490 N/m, assuming the standard 500 gf/cm load), every fabric picks +1.0 cm, the 2D chain's answer, with every margin certified by the stopping rule. So the 3D-against-2D disagreement is a soft-cloth effect. A post hoc power-law fit to LT and WT puts the suiting and the elastane jersey well inside the settled regime at the garment's own shoulder load (tangent 1,300 to 6,200 N/m), but the cotton jersey (250 to 370 N/m) and the shirting (700 to 1,050 N/m) in the band where the choice flips. Settling them needs the low-load toe of the tensile curve, not the KES summary numbers. Milestone 5 proves the planned margin bound: the reference-tier regret of a cheap tier’s choice is at most the spread of the paired tier error across designs (max e − min e), not its size, and a choice is certified when the cheap tier’s margin exceeds that spread (or a Lipschitz cone of it). On the 50 tier pairs milestones 1b to 1d recorded, the 2D chain’s error against the 3D sheet (up to 1.6 to 2.0 cm) spreads 0.6 to 1.3 cm across widths, ten times the chain’s margins, so no 2D choice is certified even though its realised regret is small (mean 0.03 cm, at most 0.20 cm); only a stretch-stiffness guess of 3200 N/m against the KES-sourced value is certified (2 or 3 of 4 fabrics). The cheap tier screens out a median 3 of 7 widths but cannot judge the rest; the reference tier is still our own sheet, not a validated solver. Milestone 5b keeps the cheap tier’s own penalty: the regret is at most maxd [K |d − d̂| − (st(d) − st(d̂))], with K the slope of the paired error around the choice. On the 2D chain the realised regret is a median 34% of that bound against 12% of milestone 5’s; with K estimated from three reference runs it covers the regret in 47 of 50 tier pairs (all 50 with K doubled). A screen-and-verify loop built on it finds the reference optimum in 48 of 50 pairs with 3.9 of 7 reference runs (mean regret 0.0010 cm against 0.0022 for the best of the three runs and 0.028 for trusting the cheap tier); its two misses are the softest cloth (EA 40 N/m), whose optimum is two grid steps from the cheap choice. Milestone 3a writes ARCSim’s element model (constant-strain triangles with stretch and measured KES shear as separate parameters, discrete-shell hinge bending, a Newton solver with a coloured finite-difference Hessian) as a candidate top tier. It matches the exact heavy-cantilever elastica (the basis of ASTM D1388’s 41.5° rule) to within 0.9% of the overhang after first-order extrapolation, and stretch stiffness moves the cantilever by under 0.31%. But it fails the simulated Cusick acceptance test: on the suiting the drape coefficient still climbs about 0.016 per mesh refinement and 0.034 from EA 800 to 3200 N/m (40% less than the spring sheet), and on the soft jersey it converges only at EA 150 N/m, near the jersey’s sourced tangent stiffness, and locks above it, so constant-strain triangles are not the top tier. Milestone 3b continues each stiff case from the soft equilibrium instead of a cold start: all 40 cases converge, and at the jersey’s own sourced tangent stiffness (254 and 369 N/m) the drape coefficient moves by only 0.008 to 0.011 from a 3.75 to a 2.5 mm lattice and by 0.003 from 150 to 369 N/m, so 3a’s jersey “locking” was mostly unconverged solves, and the element passes the acceptance test there. The suiting at its sourced 1,341 and 1,896 N/m misses the 0.03 mesh bar by 0.004 to 0.006 through a change from 6 to 7 folds, and the same case can settle in fold patterns whose drape coefficients differ by up to 0.32, so calibration against a measured drape will need the measured node count too.
